[h1]▶️Introduction[/h1]
Grand Theft Auto III, or as most of us call it, GTA3, is an open-world, third-person crime game taking place in the early 2000s. All of the events happen in Liberty City. Liberty City which is based upon cities known for gang activity and crime, like Detroit and Philadelphia. Lastly, I should mention that GTA3 is the first mainstream, 3D open-world game, which is still a formula of success.

[h1]🎮Gameplay[/h1]
As mentioned above, GTA3 is the grandfather of modern games. We see more and more games opt in for an open-world setting because of the success that the Grand Theft Auto series had. Having never played this GTA installment, I decided to play through it more than twenty years after release and see how it holds up.

Let's start with the open-world mechanics, as they were the highlight of this game. Liberty City still feels like a dynamic place. People walk around in a funny and animatronic manner, with vehicles going around city streets, planes gliding through the sky and boats dashing through the waves. The result of that randomness gives the sensation and atmosphere of a life-like city with how things are going. Of course, being the protagonist will also get you the chance to take part in various activities and missions. You discover more areas of the map by progressing throughout the story. Keep in mind that with every new part of the city, you will be able to complete side missions and mini-games.Talking about missions, most of them are well crafted. Their design is  simple, go to point A, steal or kill your target and return to base. That may sound easy, but in practice, it can get a lot more entertaining and challenging! The variety of the missions also helps in keeping you engaged. Every mission has a different theme or agenda behind it, sometimes you drive in a win or lose race, and other times you start a gang war with the Chinese. That is a very strong aspect of this game.

https://youtu.be/CJeIqOmgMRk

Being a fantastic sandbox it allows you to waste time on this game. Fighting against the police with your comically large inventory is a classic gaming moment. Stealing a nice sports car and exploring Liberty City is something everyone should do.

The shooting mechanics have aged badly, which isn't a surprise. Aiming might feel rusty and unresponsive, especially with a scoped weapon. Hit reg is also abysmal, although it is excusable due to the age.

[h1]🎭Story[/h1]
[h2]This review contains no spoilers.[/h2]
Something to be expected is that the story has a lot to do with crimes, backstabbing and revenge. You being a silent protagonist makes the entire story hit or miss. You never see Claude react to much at all. He feels programmed and stoic. It might seem like a terrible aspect, but at the same time, it makes everything seem deeper story-wise. I found myself constantly wondering about Claude's motives because of his mysterious and quiet persona. The other characters presented throughout the story are memorable and also impactful. The entire plot gave me the idea that there is always a risk, someone you trust will betray you for their own personal gain. On your journey to redemption you do the same to others that helped you and use them as a tool. I am avoiding spoilers but these are the motives of the story to my understanding.


I spent 15 hours with the game, which is a decent time. Considering how engaging the events are, I would easily consider the story as another strength of this title.

Another game that I am a more than a decade late playing...Grand Theft Auto 3 was released in mid 2002; and is actually the fifth game in the GTA series, however this game was the one which changed the franchise into the series we know today. 

The game is set in the fictional city of Liberty City, which is actually loosely based on New York City. You play the role of a bank robber named Claude, and you become entrapped in a world of gangsters and corruption very quickly.  This was the first GTA game to change from the topdown view of the previous titles and move to a third person view - which combined the a new third-person and driving experience in a new game engine. 

In GTA III we have the main story line, in which you can pick and choose which missions to complete for certain characters. Many of the missions are not mandatoy to move the story forward however. You can carry out smaller side activities such as being a taxi for the night, or hijacking an ambulance resucing people and dropping them off at the hospital.

The graphics are dated but it is over ten years old, what were you expecting? You can get graphically enhancing community made mods to increase the fidelity a bit too. I personally really like these dated looking graphics.

GTA III will challenge you at points; more so that you will probably end up dying quite a bit. Some missions require a lot of shooting and evading police, while others involve a little bit of parkour and trying not to just kill yourself in a stupid manner. The re-spawn system is very good in GTA though; you loose all your weapons as well as having to pay a fee for the hospital having to patch you up. 

As you can see, I have over a hundred hours in GTA III, this is through having multiple playthroughs, as well as completing the game 100% on a number of occasions; however this past week I did a full playthrough of the story and a couple of the side activities and this took me almost twelve hours to complete. There is a ton more content to play in that playthrough too, so you can easily get about fifteen plus hours out of one playthrough of GTA III if you desire. 

Oddly enough I had no real game breaking technical issues with GTA III, the only one I did find is it is not recommended to play this game with more than one monitor activated at a time, as your mouse will sometimes wander out of the game window and you will end up minimizing your game all the time. To be honest though; just the one issue on a ten year old game is pretty good going if you ask me. 

In conclusion, GTA III is a land mark in gaming history; it is the game which revolutionized the GTA series, sparked media controversy, and most of all, gave us one of the best games in history. Most will have already completed this game; however if you haven't - I strongly advise you dust your copy off and give it a weekend of your time to play.

GTA III took the foundations that were GTA 1 & GTA 2 and doubled down. It was my most anticipated game of 2001.

The freedom was GTA III's major selling point.
"You don't have to do any of the missions"
"You can go where you like"
"You can do whatever you want"
The pitch was you had a fully-rendered 3D city to explore. That was the draw -- the appeal. There were little to no games like it at the time. It was revolutionary.

I'll use an example.

Sleeping Dogs, a cult favourite, wouldn't exist without the True Crime series, and those games wouldn't exist without GTA III's very existence.

Saints Row is getting a reboot as I write this review. That series was made at a time where there was no new GTA title. Saints Row 1 was clearly inspired by San Andreas, which was the series swansong for that generation. It took everything GTA III and Vice City had an perfected it. Open world games today would never play the way they do without GTA III's influence. GTA III inspired a generation of games and arguably revolutionised the open-world genre in general.

I have a lot of respect for GTA III.

Sure, it's nowhere near as cram-filled full of things to do as later games in the series, but it paved the way, and to those people who are complaining that there is no GTA VI being announced and regard GTA III as the worst in the series; do yourself a favour and put yourself in the shoes of someone living in 2001 and think to yourself "it'll never get better than this", because it did, and you have GTA III to thank for it.

Grand Theft Auto III revolutionized open world gaming, setting a new standard for freedom, immersion, and ambition. For the first time, players were dropped into a fully realized 3D city Liberty City where they could steal any car, cause chaos, or simply wander and soak in the atmosphere. The combination of a crime driven narrative, sandbox freedom, and immersive radio stations created a living, breathing world that felt unlike anything before it. Liberty City is gritty and atmospheric, buzzing with pedestrians, traffic, and dynamic events that made it feel alive. Whether you were exploring back alleys, hijacking cars, or just listening to the in-game radio’s mix of music and parody talk shows, the city had an authenticity and energy that pulled players in. That said, some aspects haven’t aged gracefully. The shooting mechanics feel clunky by modern standards, the driving can be overly stiff, and the mission design occasionally leans into trial and error frustration. Still, these flaws are easy to forgive when you remember the scale of what the game accomplished at the time. Its impact on gaming cannot be overstated. GTA III paved the way not only for future entries in the series, but for the entire open-world genre as we know it today. Countless games have borrowed from its blueprint of freedom, crime, and urban exploration. While later entries improved upon the formula in nearly every way, GTA III remains a classic worth revisiting both as a piece of gaming history and as a reminder of just how groundbreaking it was when it first hit the PS2.

I'm going to describe that time period in details, so if you want to hear the rest - make sure you've got a big cup of tea. The story will be long, and it even has a plot twist. Man, how many lessons were skipped, how many exams were failed, how many once happy and serene families were ruined by this game... People really lost their mind about this game. Back then it even overshadowed CS 1.3 (wink). Inside, many of them were rather dirty and had rather dense stench of cheap alcohol, bad tobacco and unwashed bodies. Entering some of them was like entering some cyberpunk reality, because those places were rather, lets say, spicy. They attracted "elite" from the very bottom of society who were openly trading with, hmm, all sorts of unconventional stuff. Thus, parents could rest assured that their kids are in reliable hands, hehe.

You are still on board? - Very well. Because here comes another touching passage about my acquaintance with GTA franchise, before I'll head for the conclusions about GTA3... Cold autumn of 1997. A friend of mine brought me a bunch of his discs with video games. One and a half dozen or so. Why? Da hell I know. I tried to remember but nothing substantive comes to my mind. So, what are those games? - garbage (it may partially explain my friend's generosity as well). It didn't take much time for me to put them into this cathegory. 

In this pile of trash, one game specifically grabbed my attention. Why? Because among all this garbage, this one looked even worse than garbage: broken box inside and outside, broken plastic, frontal screen was torn and dirty as if he wiped something with it... So I tried to read some illegible description... dma design (nothing ringed the bell - probably developers?)... steal cars, shoot stuff, bla-bla... oh! the game's name - Grandfather Auto?... what the hell, sounds stupid - let me check it. Launched the game - ah, so that's Grand Theft Auto!

It turned out that the game was a blast. I spent maybe a week before I bothered to check the first mission, coz all this time I was just driving and shooting stuff while listening cool music. Stupid or not, but I had a lot of fun playing like that. Later on I started to fulfill actual missions, discovered paint workshops, secrets, hidden missions - great and unique experience for those times. 

Year after year, 2002nd has arrived. And GTA3 was released. And something unimaginable happend. Total disaster. The end of the world was at hand - my PC could not run GTA3... Are you crying with me? Incurable wound was inflicted and despair was absolute. Thus, I found salvation in the arms of Mafia. Mafia... worked on my PC.

Outcome is close, so check your belts... A year later I got top PC. The time has come to get what I was denied before. And GTA3 was №1 on my revenge list. So I played it. And I had some fun. At the same time though because there have been so many games based off it, it occasionally feels like it lacks an identity compared to the glut of sandbox games that came after it. 

This is fundamentally the base game that all future sandbox games jumped off from. It's a game I like to go back to every so often to remind myself where it all started. And to remind myself that Rockstar set the bar pretty high from the start and just kept going from there.

Grand Theft Auto III is the more or less revolutionary, third major entry into the open-ended criminal sandbox game series, spanning from 1997's original top down entry. You play as an unnamed man in this game - later games give him the name of Claude - who seeks revenge from their former partner in crime after they betrayed and left them for dead during a job gone wrong.

By today's standards the game looks positively... poor, but for a 2001 title in an industry still reluctantly stepping into full-fledged 3D graphics, it was astonishing. Nevertheless, character models are pretty obviously composed of separated segments that are animated as need be, often wonkily and even in cutscenes, and while the draw distance is impressive for a game of its age, props and entities still obviously spawn just a short distance ahead of where you look. Small details litter the game world and help in grounding you into its satirical yet dreary and hostile-feeling atmosphere, but it does little when the big picture itself looks dated.

Audio is notably low quality, especially for voice acting, but there is good variety in sound effects, from weapons to vehicles. The radio feature remains a (relatively speaking, anyway) unspoken-of piece of brilliance: 9 radio stations, featuring a wide range of musical genres, and one hilarious talk radio show, to be listened to from any civilian vehicle. Unlike future entries, the humour in dialogue is toned down during mission cutscenes, and mostly relegated either to the radio or to random passerbys spouting nonsense on the streets.

Gameplay is understandably the meat of the game. As a transition from the top-down gameplay to full 3D, some quirks remain to tide over players of the original games, including an optional top-down camera view not seen in any future mainline games, gaining money for fender benders and exploding cars, and the protagonist actually being mute and only partaking in one-way conversations with people, generally to receive mission objectives. The missions have fair variety in delivery of a narrow set of objectives, but quickly become [b]annoying[/b]. Future GTA games are graced with things like a map screen, waypoints, more detailed and clear objectives and locations, autosaves, journey skips and mid-mission checkpoints. This game has none of that bar a useful but really restricted minimap in the corner, which doesn't even have a good coloring scheme to distinguish water from roads or tunnels. 

Missions are also made that much more annoying by being given no indication of which missions permanently disable performing others until you fulfill them or consult a walkthrough.. nor that, as the storyline progresses, gangs become permanently hostile with you, including a mafia wielding very dangerous weapons that can blow your car up or knock you out to the hospital in a few seconds. You also have a (barebones, by modern GTA standards) list of side activities to perform that reward you with in-game money and additional perks, ranging from being a taxi driver, ambulance driver or "vigilante" officer (providing a souped-up cab, health pickups and wanted level clearing bribes, respectively), to entering certain vehicles parked in specific locations that trigger minigames, and the usual assortment of "hidden package" collectibles that grant an ever expanding armory at your safehouses, which is a godsend when seemingly every other mission wants to screw you over in a flaming wreck, or just end you from onslaughts of enemies who can stun you out of shooting a tiny bit (a lot if shotgun) when you get hit.

For smaller things that can throw off even established players of newer GTA games, a big one is the car handling. They have a much wider range of variation in stats (who'd have thought a lowly looking estate can turn so quickly?) but most end up feeling like they can tip over from just taking a corner at moderate velocity. There's also NO MID-AIR CAR CONTROL, which screws you over 9 times out of 10 if you take a jump or fall badly. Land on your roof? You better crawl out of there fast. You also cannot dive out of a moving car, so you have to come to a stop - again, even as it's about to blow up. All vehicles have much more vague damage indication: while body panels come off with the slightest touch and isn't too unusual for GTA games of its era, vehicles will get some puffs of white smoke coming from the engine after unspecified and seemingly random amounts of damage... then at some point finally go "oh it's fire now, better run", with no further warning of a vehicle's damage state. Weapons have a progression system which amounts to: the pistol is useless the moment you get an Uzi, which is almost useless the moment you get an AK, which is thoroughly useless the moment you get an M16, which is only a notch below the Bazooka, and the shotgun is a poor man's Bazooka for up to 15ft (and also Claude's kryptonite).

Oh yeah, and you can't swim. The action takes place in and around two islands and one mainland segment, and boats are finnicky enough to line up to jetties and hop off as it is, so there's that.

There is easily content for dozens of hours of play in one go, and possibly hundreds more if you're bent on completing the coveted 100% Completion checklist, but this game is not for the faint of heart. Even having played newer titles in the series, III is a monster of its own. Its scale is much smaller and its delivery confusing/confused, but you'll be flipping walkthrough pages the most for this game. [spoiler]okay, the most right after San Andreas[/spoiler] Enter this then amazing, now bizarre gem of gaming, and those who can stomach it will have a pretty good time.

I could write just one word here and call it a day: REVOLUTIONARY.

This game had mediocre graphics, iffy physics, uninspired storyline and it ran badly even on some powerful PCs. It was undeniably rushed, with a plethora of bugs popping up left and right. They didn't even bother to put a roof on most of the buildings, assuming no one will see it (they were wrong)... These are actual complaints frequently repeated back in the day.

And yet, this game has redefined the term "sandbox" into what we know it as today. It didn't excel at any aspect... but it just made a darn good use of all what it had. It really felt like the most complete and realistic simulation of a gangster yet. Wreaking havoc has never been so satisfying before.

At the time, the possibilities appeared endless. The city seemed huge beyond imagination, I could spend hours just driving around listening to the radio. There's nothing you couldn't do - you could have multiple apartments, save cars in a garage, fly a plane, drive a boat, annihilate surroundings with a tank, work as a cab driver, paramedic, firefighter or even a cop (!). Not to mention the map was filled up to the brim with collectibles and other minor secrets.

Many people despised the dull and grim looks of the Liberty City. To me, it is fitting. Unlike many of the sequels, in this entry the city is dark and often shrouded in fog. This really makes for an distinctive atmosphere.

Even though the graphics as a whole failed to impress, there were so many little quirks it really caught your attention. You could rip out car panels. Doors could open on impact (which would then flap around as you drove in the corners), and the protagonist would attempt to close them. Cars could spawn in several variants, for example as a cabriolet or hardtop. You could dismember pedestrians - a feature that was removed from the subsequent games. There were leaves and old newspapers floating around. Rockstar has also implemented a day and night cycle and various weather conditions, making the virtual world ever so immersive.

The soundtrack is superb, it's definitely one of the things that made GTAIII so special. I love the fact that the radio stations were composed mostly from music produced specifically for this game. It's really a shame that Rockstar has dropped this approach in the newer games (aside from Liberty City Stories, which also featured a truly unique and memorable soundtrack).

As with any GTA, this game doesn't take itself very seriously. The humour is spot on. I especially love the chat radio stations, they always end up talking about such nonsense crap it keeps me in stitches.

If I had to pick one thing about this game that has aged the worst, it'd definitely be the plot and missions. The main storyline is just a typical "betrayed man who seeks revenge" scenario with little to no unexpected plottwists. The missions mostly revolve around transporting the item/person, collecting items, killing someone, driving from point A to point B... This was perfectly acceptable at the time, but now it feels barren. Even the big finale doesn't really stand out from the rest.
Also, the main protagonist is completely silent. While I like that it makes him much more intriguing and mysterious (and some say this makes him easier to relate to), I really do feel like this was a wasted opportunity. Take a look at the sequels - characters like Tommy Vercetti, Carl Johnson, etc. are unforgettable. Claude just isn't.

Any way you look at it, it's a classic, a truly groundbreaking title. For me, this is by far the most nostalgic entry in the series. No other game made a bigger impression on me and none ever will. To be honest though, Vice City improved on pretty much every aspect and if you've never played III before, I doubt you'd enjoy it today. But if you can stomach it not being as good as Vice City, it's definitely recommended.
Genuinely one of the most influential and important games of the last few decades. A true classic in every sense of the word.

[h1][b]Overview[/b][/h1]
Grand Theft Auto 3 is an open world action-adventure game that shifted the industry by bringing the series into a fully realized 3D city. Set in the crime-ridden Liberty City, players rise through the criminal underworld by completing missions for various factions while freely exploring the city between objectives. Rather than relying on a single gameplay gimmick, it combines driving, third-person shooting, exploration, and emergent sandbox chaos into one experience. Although many of its ideas have since become genre standards, its historical importance and freedom still make it appealing to players interested in classic open world design and gaming history.

[h1][b]Gameplay[/b][/h1]
The core gameplay loop revolves around accepting missions, traveling across Liberty City, completing objectives, and unlocking new districts. Outside of story missions, players are free to steal vehicles, evade police, search for hidden collectibles, or simply explore the city.

Driving remains the strongest mechanic, with a varied selection of vehicles that each feel distinct despite simplified physics. Gunplay, however, reflects the game's age. Combat lacks modern conveniences such as manual aiming refinement or a cover system, making firefights feel clunky by today's standards. Controls can also feel stiff, particularly during on-foot movement.

Mission variety is respectable, ranging from assassinations and races to timed deliveries and large shootouts. Difficulty fluctuates noticeably, with certain missions becoming frustrating because of limited checkpoints and unforgiving failure conditions rather than genuine mechanical depth.

Exploration is consistently rewarding thanks to the dense city layout, hidden shortcuts, and memorable neighborhoods. While progression remains straightforward, the sandbox provides enough freedom to create memorable unscripted moments even decades after release.

[h1][b]Story & World[/b][/h1]
The narrative is intentionally simple, focusing on betrayal, revenge, and the pursuit of power within Liberty's criminal hierarchy. The silent protagonist limits emotional depth, yet it allows supporting characters to take center stage. Crime bosses, gang leaders, and corrupt figures each leave a distinct impression through well-written dialogue and memorable personalities.

Liberty City itself is arguably the true star. Every district has a unique atmosphere, architecture, and social identity, making exploration feel meaningful. The story moves at a brisk pace and avoids unnecessary exposition, though character development is relatively limited compared to later entries in the series.

[h1][b]Visual Presentation[/b][/h1]
Viewed through a modern lens, the graphics are undeniably dated, with low-polygon character models, simple textures, and basic animations. However, the artistic direction remains effective. Liberty City captures a bleak urban atmosphere through its industrial environments, weather effects, and distinctive districts.

Lighting and visual effects are modest but contribute to the overall mood. The interface is clean and functional, although some menus show their age. While realism is limited, the game's visual identity continues to hold historical and artistic value.

[h1][b]Audio[/b][/h1]
Audio is one of Grand Theft Auto 3's greatest strengths. The radio stations feature an excellent mix of music, satirical advertisements, and talk shows that give Liberty City its personality. Environmental sounds, vehicle engines, and weapon effects reinforce immersion throughout gameplay.

Voice acting is consistently strong, with performances that add credibility to the criminal cast. Dialogue remains entertaining without overstaying its welcome, and the sound design helps make the world feel alive despite technical limitations.

[h1][b]Performance & Technical Quality[/b][/h1]
On modern PC hardware, performance is generally excellent thanks to the game's modest requirements. Loading times are short, and crashes are uncommon with the official release, although compatibility quirks may appear depending on operating systems or hardware configurations.

The PC version offers basic graphical options, but they are limited compared to modern standards. Technical shortcomings mostly stem from the games age rather than severe instability, though camera behavior and controls can occasionally create avoidable frustration.

[h1][b]Content & Replayability[/b][/h1]
The main story offers roughly 15 to 20 hours of content, with additional time available through side activities, hidden packages, stunt jumps, rampages, and optional vehicle missions. There is no New Game+ or multiplayer component.

Replayability remains respectable thanks to player freedom, multiple approaches to exploration, and achievement hunting. While the amount of optional content is smaller than later GTA titles, there is still enough to encourage revisiting Liberty City.

[h1][b]Value for Money[/b][/h1]
As the original PC version is no longer available for purchase on Steam, its value largely depends on how players already own or access it. Those who purchased it before its removal still have access to a complete single-player experience with no microtransactions or paid gameplay expansions. While newer open world games offer more content and modern conveniences, Grand Theft Auto 3 remains a historically significant title whose sandbox design continues to be rewarding for players interested in revisiting a landmark of the genre.

[h1][b]Pros[/b][/h1]
• Groundbreaking open world freedom that remains enjoyable.
• Memorable city design with strong atmosphere.
• Excellent soundtrack, radio stations, and voice acting.
• Varied mission structure and rewarding exploration.
• Strong historical importance within the genre.
• Smooth performance on most modern PCs.

[h1][b]Cons[/b][/h1]
• Combat and controls feel dated.
• Mission difficulty can be inconsistent.
• Limited character development due to the silent protagonist.
• Basic graphics and animations show their age.
• Few quality-of-life features expected from modern games.
• Limited graphics customization on PC.

[h1][b]Final Verdict[/b][/h1]
Grand Theft Auto 3 remains one of the most influential games ever released. While many mechanics have aged and newer entries surpass it in nearly every technical category, its open world design, immersive city, and sense of player freedom still make it an engaging experience. It is best approached as both a classic game and an important milestone in the evolution of sandbox design. Players willing to accept its dated mechanics will find a landmark title that continues to earn its reputation.

[b]Final Score: 86/100[/b]

Every legend begins somewhere, and Grand Theft Auto III is the game that laid the foundation not only for the entire GTA series as we know it today, but in many ways for the entire open-world sandbox structure of games that continue to enjoy popularity.  It's been said that this game pales in comparison to the games that would come later in the 'GTA III trilogy', namely Vice City and San Andreas.  While it's true that those games further refined and expanded upon the GTA experience in important ways, the essential building blocks for those changes were created here in GTA III.

I've trumped up the historical importance of the game a bit but the question remains as to whether the gameplay in GTA III has held up, especially in relation to the later iterations in the series.  Thankfully I can answer that with a resounding, "Yes!"  So let's talk about some of the things that make this game tick.  First and foremost, we have the story.  In GTA III Rockstar was pinning down some of the aspects that would come to be regarded as the Rockstar style of storytelling.  The story here is basically a love letter to latter day crimeland movies like Goodfellas, Heat, Donnie Brasco, Reservoir Dogs, and the like.  In this capacity all the requisite pieces are in play, including the Italian mafia, Japanese yakuza, Chinese triads, as well a healthy assortment of street level thugs.  You are a mute protagonist (who we would later know as Claude thanks to GTA: San Andreas), making a name for himself on the back of jobs from all these various criminal factions.  Naturally there are betrayals, double-crosses, hits and feints between all of these organizations, and Rockstar handles its authorial pen deftly enough to keep the story moving at a good pace.  The whole story has the tone and feel of a pulp crime movie you might see as part of a matinee crime movie marathon; nothing of great substance, but a whole lot of fun nevertheless.

In GTA III we also see the beginnings of Rockstar's tendency to include well-known actors performing voice work in their games.  Here we have Michael Madsen, Joe Pantoliano, Michael Rappaport, Debi Mazar, Kyle MacLachlan, and gangster movie legend Frank Vincent all playing supporting roles in the game.  The caliber of voice acting in this game really does some great things for the conveyance of the story.  In the hands of lesser actors, certain aspects of this story might have come off as laughably cringe-worthy.  As it is we are treated to voice work performed by old pros, particularly where crime drama is concerned.

Here we are also treated to the first GTA game to include an absolutely killer soundtrack complete with genre specific radio stations, distinct DJs for each radio station, and some great licensed music.  It had been quite a few years since I played this game, and these tunes (as well as spoken dialog) really filled me with a sense of nostalgia.  In truth it's the radio stations that give this game its comedic timing and fantastically dark sense of humor.  As an added bonus, the PC port of this game allows you create a custom playlist of mp3s which can be imported into the game.  I really had a great time importing my own tunes into the game.  Once you do so, the 'MP3 Player' becomes selectable in any vehicle just like a normal radio station which plays your tracks on random repeat.  Let me tell you that you haven't lived until you've gone on a drive-by rampage with Electric Wizard's Funeralopolis blaring from the sound system of your Patriot.  >=D

The gameplay mechanics are admittedly somewhat long in the tooth at this point, but even still they are pretty darned enjoyable.  The drifty, somewhat floaty driving mechanics that are a hallmark of 3D GTA games make their debut here.  At first the driving might seem a slightly off, being that I don't know of any other driving game that handles quite like the GTA games.  The handling is a bit loose, but once you get that part dialed in it's a real blast.  Of course the looseness of vehicle handling depends a lot on what vehicle you're in at any given time.  It does need to be said that there are no motorcycles in GTA III, which for me is perhaps one aspect of the later games that I missed the most here.  There are also no helicopters, and only one (notoriously difficult to control) aircraft.  That said, the variety of vehicles available here is suited well to the game, and I feel that the slightly limited selection of vehicles can be forgiven being that we are talking about the first GTAs first foray into full 3D.

This was my first play though of the Steam PC port of GTA III, and I will say that I found some relatively minor issues with the port.  First and foremost, the aiming mechanics were … problematic for me in this version.  In the 'Classic Control' scheme, the relatively responsive nature of the auto-targeting feature found in the console version of the game just doesn't carry over very well in the PC version.  It fails to reliably switch between targets, and in many cases it fails to [i]find[/i] any targets at all (despite the fact that said targets are in the process of filling you with lead).  Furthermore, when you're using the Classic Control scheme the right thumb stick puts you in first person look perspective rather than adjusting the 3rd person camera as one might expect.  Others may have had a slightly different experience with Classic Mode controls, but for me the combination of the above factors made this option a non-starter.  The 'Standard Control' scheme makes some marked improvements to the above, but in this case you're stuck strictly with free aiming.  I tend to prefer keyboard & mouse controls for games that require free aiming, and indeed given that strafing features prominently into the Standard Control scheme in GTA III, one might assume that KB+M is what the developers had in mind here … except that KB+M makes driving nearly impossible (although not [i]entirely[/i] impossible as I do know at least one person that beat this game entirely with KB+M).  Using the Standard Control scheme, I ultimately ended up ruling in favor of using a controller to better facilitate driving, although I did find a helpful mod that made this option a bit more feasible.  The [url=http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=172881491]GInput mod[/url] allows you to fully utilize an Xinput device in GTA III which makes using a controller in the game a bit more palatable, and has the added benefit of additional customizable settings.  It even swaps out correct button icons for onscreen prompts.  So there's that.

On my (Nvidia-based) gaming rig there were also a couple of graphical glitches present in this port.  Most noticeably I encountered the 'dark vehicles' glitch, in which all the vehicles appear to have a much darker tint than they should.  For this issue I applied a second light weight user-made patch to the game which resolved the issue promptly.  If you find yourself with the same problem, [url=http://forums.steampowered.com/forums/showthread.php?t=1859227]this fix[/url] is probably worth your time as well.

At the end of the day, the question is whether or not this game is still worth your time.  Given the popularity (and occasional notoriety) enjoyed by the GTA series, you probably already know whether the source material is your cup of tea.  Dark comedy, violence, and debauchery abound!  If you're already a fan of the series, or if you're looking to get into the 3D era of GTA games at the ground floor, I would say that this game still holds a lot of enjoyment even today.  It had been a number of years since I last played this game and I enjoyed it a lot more than I expected I would especially given the historical perspective of subsequent GTA games.  This old jalopy has still got some life in 'er yet!

It was probably good in 2001. Having played through the whole thing in 2021 (my first time completing it, though not my first time playing it), I don't think it's aged well. By "completing" I mean doing all the main story missions, all the payphone missions, and collecting the hidden packages. Not bothering with the taxi stuff.

The AI vehicles often spawn in walls or crash into each other for no reason. I assume the developers were proud to figure out how to make the AI change lanes after four hours of caffeine coding, so they made all the AI vehicles change lanes every 5 seconds, not caring if that means they will crash into your car while you're driving at 120 miles per hour right past them (this is especially noticeable on the big bridges and in the tunnels). The game is not optimized for newer machines and assumes you are playing on a 1940s computer because cars will despawn when you look away from them if they're more than 5 meters away. If you play above 30Hz your car will not reverse in at least the first mission. And I had a problem with the menu options being too transparent when I started, don't remember how I fixed it though.

The story is okay but overrated. Ok, so Claude is a psychopath and will kill anyone as long as he gets money for it? Kinda lazy, I don't care for the guy at all. Much of the game, especially the third or so before the Mafia part, is just random "go do this for me" filler missions to make the game seem longer. And some of the missions are only available at certain times of day, so you just sit there on your phone until the in-game clock hits a certain time; fortunately, this only happens in Portland.

The game is very difficult to enjoy after you progress through most of the missions as random gang members all around the map will start shooting you. Yes, they even notice you if you're zooming past them in a vehicle, and your car blows up after taking a few bullets, in fact if you stub your toe against the car it will blow up. This makes many of the side missions needlessly difficult if you don't do them before the gang members turn hostile. It also makes most of the map unexplorable, especially the north half of Portland where you will just be insta-killed by angry Mafia members with shotguns. Speaking of the map, you don't actually get a map. You're supposed to "get used to it and memorize the city" as some bitter old man who I am paraphrasing said online when I looked up where I'm supposed to buy guns (it's not marked on the mini-map), yeah let me memorize the whole city with a squad of gang guys every 10 feet shooting at me. Prepare to use Google images a lot.

And the game just hasn't aged that well. You can't turn your camera while driving, I guess that's alright since there are buttons to reverse the camera and look at a fixed 90 degree left and right view but it takes a while to get used to. The guns are almost humorously inaccurate, you can aim a shotgun at someone from a few feet away and take four shots before you actually hit them once. And I am talking about alcohol shots because this game will make you a depressed alcoholic. At least one of the assault rifles rapid fires an accurate straight line of bullets, but they go slightly above and to the right of the cross-hair. If you die, you will lose all the guns you paid for, but that's okay because all you need to do is collect 100 hidden packages so the guns spawn at your safehouse, but don't worry, the game won't tell you which ones you've collected so if you use a guide and miss one you have to go through all of them again, just to complete some of the harder missions without contemplating premature real life expiration because of the lack of a sniper rifle. I should also add that, if you die at any point in a mission, you have to restart the mission from scratch, and I mean from the hospital walking all the way back to the mission giver. Great stuff!

The only good things I will give this game are the selection of music and the world design. But the world design doesn't even matter because you can't explore it without constantly being shot by the Colombian cartel.

So, I'm going to not recommend it, unless you fall into one of the following three groups: (1) old-school GTA fans who want to play the mediocre game they remember only through their flawed nostalgia glasses, (2) completionists like me who just want to play through every GTA game when they could be doing something more productive instead, (3) GTA VI developers who are required by Rockstar to play this so they know how to not make a GTA game. Note that fitting into one these groups does not mean you will actually enjoy the game.

Anyway I hope Vice City is better.

Grand Theft Auto III is one of the most revolutionary games ever made, it changed the video game landscape forever, so let's get into it.

We play as Claude, a young bank robber who is trying to make it in Liberty City. After a bank heist his girlfriend Catalina shoots Claude and leaves him for dead. After a prison break Claude escapes and so begins his quest for revenge towards Catalina.

The gameplay is pretty identical to every other GTA game, but I'll explain if you want to know. The game is a sandbox title where you are free to explore at your own pace, you can travel by foot, by car or by boat. No air travel just yet. It's fun driving around and seeing the sights in Liberty City.

The gameplay is very stiff for this title. The driving is very hard to control and requires a lot of time getting used to it, but once you're used to it, it's not big of a problem. 

The game also has a mission structure and every mission requires to do a lot of different stuff, ranging from racing, to hitman missions and a lot more stuff. A lot of the missions can be fun, but a lot of them are incredibly difficult and here is the biggest problem with the game.

Now don't get me wrong, when a game is challenging that is not bad, but when it's so hard it's next to the point of being unfair is not good. GTA Vice City and San Andreas has a good mixture of difficulty where the missions where possible no matter what. GTA 3 however is incredibly difficult due to the very confusing objective placements and really punishing missions where a few good placed shots could blow up your car.

The soundtrack is also really lackluster. Every radio station only has 4 songs each ( at least from what I remember). But a lot of the songs are good, so I won't go too harsh on it.

The story is really great, while not the best thing of all time, it helps to push you to the conclusion and it really satisfies you after the end credits start rolling.

While playing, I had zero issues with the game. No crashes, no game breaking bugs. Apart from minor AI glitches, I had no problems.

The game took me 13 hours to finish, after you're done, you also have races and packages you can collect all over Liberty City.

Overall GTA 3 is a good game, but it has not aged well since 2001. It's a revolutionary game and I won't deny the impact it had on the world of gaming, but I highly suggest players to buy either Vice City or San Andreas.

Final Rating:
6/10 - Worth Purchasing on Sale

In 2001, I was a junior in high school, and as one, was completely blown away by GTA III. The music, the size of the game, the overall gloomy rainy atmosphere - it was right up my alley. And now, 15 years later, I look back and realized that nothing has changed and that this game still remains one of my favorites. I think it's safe to say that it influenced my life quite a lot - I learned to drive while playing it; I was learning English at the time and the game helped a lot; my music tastes were influenced by the radio stations. And when I was feeling blue, like I did a lot when in high school, I could escape in this approximation of the reality across the ocean. 

Sure, these days with newer games like GTA IV and V, the graphics are better, the plot is more twisted, guns are more abundant and the music is newer/different. [b]Intro[/b]
I’m about to praise this game to Heaven and back, and I wouldn’t blame you for chalking my kind words for GTA III all up to nostalgia, but I promise I haven’t even played the game until now.

[b]The Great:[/b]
++Grand Theft Auto III's difficulty is severely exaggerated. It's a challenging game, sure, especially in comparison to the brain-dead easy GTA V (I actually do like V believe it or not lol) and as such you'll have to actually give at least half the missions in the game more than one attempt to pass, but I really
don't understand why so many of these missions are infamously difficulty within the series. Some of the supposedly hardest I managed to do in one go, even missions with timers I made mistakes in (multiple wrong turns, crashes, etc.) and yet I still got passed them in one go. The only mods I used were the SIlent Patch
to get the game running on modern platforms, the widescreen support patch and the controller support patch (which doesn't even have auto-aim), so I doubt anything made it easier.
++Vehicle handling is really enjoyable. My biggest problem with GTA V was the vehicle handling and now I realise that’s why I never enjoyed that game that much but here it’s brilliant (even if you’ll constantly flip). It’s incredibly responsive, you’ll rarely spin-out and when you get one of the fast cars, the
sense of speed is great. It’s just joyfully arcadey, which is nice since driving is without exaggeration what you’ll be doing throughout at least 80% of the time.
++The city is one of my favourites in the series. It’s easy to get around and varied enough
++Missions are really varied and well-designed. They're often short but incredibly fun. This is a bit of a back-handed compliment, but given how really not great the gunplay is, which I'm sure Rockstar knew, most missions aren't built around firefights and as a result they really let their creativity shine in
creating diverse scenarios instead of focusing on a proven formula (had the shooting been well-designed).
++This game's got a decently strong atmosphere that I love. It's dark, satirical without turning its narrative into nothing but a joke, and a joy to be immersed in.

[b]The Good:[/b]
+Graphics have held up really damn good once you get HD resolutions set-up. It's smooth yet detailed and even has some nice fake reflections here and there that still hold-up fairly well.
+Car deformation still looks pretty damn good even today. It’s more impressive than V. Seriously.
+Story-mode progressions feels rewarding as you gain access to new parts of the map and along with it new stores with new weaponry and new vehicles
+Great length to it
+The game's story is straight-forward, but it's not boring or uninteresting. The characters are likeable and well voice actored and even the mute protagonist is one seriously awesome, cold-blooded, vengeful, mercenary motherfucker.
+Sound design's good. You can tell it's GTA III just by listening to it thanks to the weird, repetitive, random NPC muttering and odd musical riffs near certain mission providers that lend to the game's slightly off atmosphere.
+The hidden collectibles, you know, those usually useless hidden items scattered around the place in every open-world game since, are actually helpful to find, as once you hit 1/10th you're granted a new very useful item at your safehouse
+Gore is awesomely brutal. Every piece of the Human body can be dismembered and decapitated with any type of weapon. It's great watching a crowd of people get blown up and have 3/4ths of their limbs removed, or to watch someone briefly hold their stump of a neck as blood pours out of their hole like a fountain.
It's sadistic in the way only video games can harmlessly entertain, and it more than makes up for the lack of ragdoll physics that make kills in the HD universe GTA games so rewarding.
+Characters are well animated, especially in cutscenes, despite character models looking like they're made-up of a more geometrically advanced version of Lego

[b]The Okay/Not Too Big of a Deal:[/b]
+-The conversational bits in the radio stations are the best bit about this game. Not even kidding. They're legitimately laugh-out-loud funny and really well written and voice-acted. The issue? The repetition is insane. You will hear the same fucking interviews over and over and you'll hear the same awful songs over and over until your ears bleed. There's about 2 songs I actually like, as well as a few musical interludes and original soundtrack stuff. The rest depresses me thinking anyone actually gets paid to produce this crap. Thankfully you can turn it off...
-+Compatibility with modern platforms sucks ass, but that's to be expected from a game from 2001... there are fantastic fan-made patches out there that make the game run perfectly on modern computers and they're easy to install. Even getting native controller support, along with on-screen correct controller prompts
and stuff like vibration support is easy to get installed.
+-Vehicles flip incredibly easily but honestly it doesn't even bother me. You're given ample time to get out of the way of them exploding (as they do once they flip) and vehicles are absolutely everywhere so you're never lost without a car. It's just something you get used to. Drive around, flip, run before it blows
up, get a new vehicle, keep going. It's just the rhythm of the game lol.
-+The gunplay as I've mentioned is pretty fucking poor. I mean, the crosshair doesn't even line up to where your shots hit at close - medium distances, but it is serviceable and it never frustrated me. In its crappiness it actually opens up different gameplay scenarios which have you
utilising long-ranged weapons and explosives in order to take out your enemies before they can really get their shots off at you. It sucks, yes, but not in a way that detracts from the actual gameplay, because the gameplay is rarely centered on the gunplay and so when it is it's a minor tactical divergence
from the other driving based objectives.

[b]The Bad:[/b]
-I really wish Pay ‘n’ Sprays and Ammunations were marked on the mini-map at all times. They’re often put in out of the way areas which can be difficult to memorise.
-Having to rebuy weapons and armour everytime you fail a mission, as well as to drive all the way back to said mission marker and then to drive to another place for the mission can get exactly as tedious as it sounds. It would've been nice to be able to just start immediately as soon as you die at mission start so you
don't waste your time, but it's not a big deal as mission markers aren't all that far away in the game world's medium size full of fast cars and smooth handling.
-There's a few extra little game modes, like side-quests from phone booths that sometimes have interaction orbs around them and sometimes don't, and sometimes lead to different missions or just replay the same ones everytime (which is annoying when you can't quit a mission without going out of your way to fail it or finish it)
and things like those set vehicles that actually force you into a whole different game mode where you're put under a timer make me wish the game told you what you're about to get into before you do. This game would've sucked for a completionist back in the day.

There are games that are core childhood memories for you, me and many gamers like us. GTA III (as well as Vice City and San Andreas) are games that defined our childhoods. In the present day, we wait with great anticipation (as well as frustration) for the release of GTA VI. Why are we all doing this? Why do we care so much? 

A big reason is because of the amazing times we had playing the original trilogy games. GTA III, San Andreas and Vice City blew our minds and captured our hearts. These games kept us glued to TV and computer screens for hours upon hours-playing by ourselves or with friends. It’s cliché to say this now but it still holds true: Liberty City, Vice City and San Andreas felt real. They weren’t just our virtual childhood playgrounds. They were living, breathing cities unlike anything we had experienced with games before.

We as gamers hope and pray that Rockstar has still got it. That they can still, through GTA VI, capture the magic of the original trilogy games. This is why we care about GTA VI and hope that it is great. 

(Note: Rockstar and Take Two have made many disappointing moves lately. Still, I am staying optimistic and keeping my fingers crossed. Should that change, I will be editing this review to reflect on my change of mind.)

When it comes to GTA III, this game opened up so many possibilities for gamers. Some of the great things GTA III did:
[olist]
[*]It showed us how much fun we could be having, especially with an open world where we could do so much more. As a child, I felt like I could do almost anything in GTA III!
[*]It showed us that games don’t have to be played mission by mission, point A to point Z, in a linear fashion.
[*]GTA III proved that games can be mature and meaningful experiences. Yes the game is quite cartoonish, especially with its portrayal of violence. But the city, and the people within it, felt alive and three dimensional. At the time it was released, GTA III proved how far games had come since the days of Pong.
[*]GTA III showed us that protagonists don’t have to be boy scouts. Claude is a silent, intimidating and violent criminal. He kills without remorse, backstabs his friends and butchers his enemies–creatingterror and carnage throughout Liberty City. Few game protagonists before Claude were like this in a game.
[*]GTA III had great voice acting from an ensemble cast of actors. Many of these actors (Michael Madsen, Robert Loggia, Frank Vincent) were famous for their roles in classic crime shows and movies. This lent credibility to GTA III as a gritty, grounded and mature piece of crime fiction–one that holds it own against the greats like Scarface or Sopranos. My personal favorite is of course Claude. HIs voice is exquisite and iconic: second only to that of Gordon Freeman!
[*]Lastly, GTA III paved the way for an entire genre of GTA clone games. Without GTA III, we would not have Mafia or Sleeping Dog (highly recommend the latter).
[/olist]

[h1] Recommendations for Specific Gamers [/h1]

[h2] First Time Players [/h2]
If you have never played the GTA trilogy games before, you should play the original games FIRST. Only then should you (if you want) touch the remasters. This is the recommended playing experience for most people.

Of course, there are exceptions:
[olist]
[*] The original games are not available from the Steam store anymore. This would be a major reason why gamers would just buy and play the Definitive Edition games.
[*]Achievement hunters [b] won’t get any achievements on Steam [/b] from playing the OG games. So they might want to skip and play the remasters. (Completionist gamers can still get 100% which they can track on the Stats screen).
[*]Some younger gamers are put off by the lack of modern graphics. This is why they don’t want to play older games. You can still use mods to improve the visual experience for the original GTA games. Try it out before you go for the remasters.
[/olist]

[h2] Music & Comedy Lovers [/h2]
One of the best parts of GTA III are its radio stations. The stations feature music tracks from a variety of genres as well as satirical comedy sketches. Driving in GTA III is so memorable because of the amazing music and the irreverent humor.

Note: Because of licensing issues, some tracks have been removed from the games on Steam. Mods are recommended to restore the experience of the original game at the time of release.

Some of my favorite radio stations on GTA III (your mileage may vary):
[olist]
[*]If you are like me, you will be laughing mad at the crazy callers on Chatterbox FM. Lazlow Jones did an amazing job with the dark comedy in the OG games. Years later, the humor in the GTA games still feels fresh (albeit a bit dated which is understandable).
[*]There are banger tracks on MSX FM and Rise FM. Both stations feature an amazing EDM tracklist full of early 2000s rave choons. Soundtrack wise, GTA III walked so the Midnight Club games could run!
[*]You will be vibing to nostalgic 80s music on Flashback FM. This station is basically a ripoff of the Scarface soundtrack!
[*]Double Clef FM has opera and classical music! Such a bold choice from Rockstar to have a station just for classical music!
[/olist]

To put it succinctly: drive whenever you can in Liberty City because you can hear the amazing radio stations!

[h2] Achievement/Completionist Hunters [/h2]
GTA III is [b]a nightmare for achievement hunters and completionists.[/b] It is possible to complete this game but it is not easy.

It is [b]highly recommended [/b] to do the following:
[olist]
[*]You should also track your game progress using [url=https://gtasnp.com] the GTA SnP website [/url].
[*]It is highly recommended to keep multiple saves as you play through this game. Keeping a backup of your saves is also good practice.
[*]Play the missions in a specific order to get 100%. This game has plenty of missable missions (about 10 or so). Keep track of those missions using guides. Again, multiple game saves will help you if you mess up.
[*]This game has known glitches that prevent getting 100%. Again, using guides can help you avoid or fix these glitches.
[/olist]

How is the completionist game experience otherwise? Collectible hunting isn't too bad with only 100 packages to collect. The vehicles for Import/Export can be a chore to find: using a guide video is recommended.

If you’re struggling to find collectibles, rampages, stunt jumps etc., use the GTASnP website as mentioned above. 

The races, stunt jumps and driving challenges are quite easy to do. I was worried about the RC planes but even they are manageable. Using a controller for vehicles is recommended. Rampages are also quite doable: you can use a mouse for aiming and shooting.

The worst part of achievement hunting are the vehicle sub missions. While Firefighter and Taxi Driver are easy to do, this is not the case for Vigilante and Paramedic. You’ll come to hate Paramedic in particular.

[h2] Paramedic Mission Haters [/h2]
Yes I am going to rant about the Paramedic missions! They are so awful they deserve their own dedicated section!
[olist]
[*]You are stuck in this fragile ambulance for [b] 12 timed missions! [/b]
[*]You get out of the ambulance, even by accident, you start over.
[*]The ambulance is easily destructible. With a little damage, it catches on fire and explodes. And then you start over.
[*]Oh by the way, there are hostile gangs which shoot at you and easily destroy your ambulance. Good luck trying to avoid them: they are on your route!
[*]Even if you avoid the gangs, you have to deal with vehicles you can easily crash into. One crash only does chip damage.
[/olist]
